newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia brings new sophistication to tax chase.
newsitem.headline: Russia brings new sophistication to tax chase.

text.p: Russian tax debtors are squirreling away funds abroad and using shell companies to avoid payments, but the State Tax Service on Wednesday said it had issued deadlines for delinquents to pay up.

Oil company Yuganskneftegaz, which may have the world's largest oil reserves, has been told to pay about $500 million by July 1 or face property seizures and seventh largest oil producer Sibneft agreed to begin payment, the service said.

The deadlines are part of government schemes to use the market to force arrears payments. After tracking down funds hidden in various schemes, Russia is requiring debtors to issue securities which the government can sell if payments dry up.

The head of the authority for enforcing tax arrears payment, Vladimir Popov, said he had uncovered sophisticated schemes by the largest tax debtors to hide earnings in intermediary companies and abroad.
"Many debtor companies use the service of intermediary firms with the goal of avoiding tax payment, using various schemes for monetary and product movement," Popov said in a statement.
But with backing from First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, the tax service has begun to force action.
Sibneft officials agreed to issue new shares to be held as collateral by the government against payment at a meeting with tax service head Alexander Pochinok and Chubais.
"A decision in principal was taken that by September 15 Sibneft should pay 1.8 trillion roubles ($310 million) by increasing its charter capital," Popov told a news conference.
Chubais has said natural gas group Gazprom, which paid off 1.3 trillion roubles in pension fund arrears by Tuesday, would pay off all its tax debts by the end of June.

Government officials have also announced schemes to force debtor regions who owe old agricultural credits and corporate delinquents to the state pension fund to issue securities to raise immediate cash, leaving the market to enforce payment.

But tax arrears by major companies grew through May 1, the latest date for which data has been released, to 32.7 trillion roubles ($5.7 billion), about one-third of the planned 1997 budget deficit, from 31.2 trillion roubles on April 1.
Harsh words in the past have not raised funds.
Popov singled out metals group Norilsk Nickel, whose main plant is a major debtor and Russia's largest auto maker, and largest tax debtor, AvtoVAZ, for avoidance schemes.

Both of the companies months ago promised to begin plans to issue new securities as collateral for debt, though Popov said if they did not take action soon, the service would begin bankruptcy proceedings.
He said Norilsk had not repatriated export earnings, a major form of capital flight and tax avoidance used by Russian companies.
It had breached currency regulations with about $600 million in transactions, but structured accounts to make the main combine "practically bereft of financial independence" he said.
AvtoVAZ used a complicated scheme of promissory notes and intermediaries to move cash revenues to an intermediary and leave its own balance sheet dominated by barter and non-cash trade, he said.
There was no comment or reaction from the companies concerned to Popov's remarks.
